facts.statement: The genus Gorgonavis contains only one species, Gorgonavis alcyone, which is known from a partial skull.
facts.quote: The genus contains a single species, Gorgonavis alcyone, known from a partial skull.

facts.statement: Gorgonavis fossils were discovered at the Las Hoyas fossil site in Cuenca, Spain.
facts.quote: The Gorgonavis fossil material was discovered at the Las Hoyas fossil site, representing outcrops of the Calizas de La Huérguina Formation, in Cuenca, Spain.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Gorgonavis is housed in the Museo Paleontológico de Castilla-La Mancha under the accession number MUPA-LH-13240.
facts.quote: The specimen is housed in the Museo Paleontológico de Castilla-La Mancha, where it is permanently accessioned as specimen MUPA-LH-13240.

facts.statement: The name Gorgonavis refers to the Gorgons of Greek mythology, specifically Medusa, due to the preservation of only an isolated skull.
facts.quote: The generic name, Gorgonavis, references the Gorgons of Ancient Greek mythology who could turn those who looked at them to stone, specifically Medusa, who was beheaded by Perseus, reminiscent of the preservation of only an isolated skull for this species.

facts.statement: The specific name alcyone comes from Greek mythology, referring to a figure transformed into a kingfisher, a bird with an elongated beak similar to Gorgonavis.
facts.quote: The specific name, alcyone, is the name of another figure in Greek mythology who was transformed into a kingfisher, a type of bird with an elongated rostrum similar to this species and other longipterygids.

facts.statement: The known fossil material consists of an isolated partial skull including the snout, lower jaw, and part of the braincase.
facts.quote: The specimen consists of an isolated partial skull, comprising the rostrum (snout region), mandible, and part of the braincase.

facts.statement: The holotype skull of Gorgonavis is approximately 3 centimeters long.
facts.quote: The holotype skull of Gorgonavis is estimated to be around 3 cm long.

facts.statement: The fused bones in the specimen indicate that the individual was skeletally mature at death.
facts.quote: The individual bones of this specimen are visibly fused, indicating this individual was likely skeletally mature when it died.

facts.statement: Three or four pairs of teeth are located in the premaxilla, a feature typical of enantiornitheans.
facts.quote: Three or four pairs of teeth are present in the premaxilla, typical for enantiornitheans.

facts.statement: The rostrum is about two and a half times the length of the eye orbit, a characteristic of longipterygids.
facts.quote: The rostrum is substantially elongated, characteristic of longipterygids, at about two-and-a-half times the orbit length.

facts.statement: The lower jaw has three visible pairs of teeth restricted to the front of the snout.
facts.quote: Like the upper jaw, there are only three visible pairs of teeth in the dentary, restricted to the front of the snout.

facts.statement: Gorgonavis lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically the Barremian age.
Gorgonavis lived approximately 129.4 million years ago and is the oldest known enantiornithean with a substantially elongated rostrum.
facts.quote: The rock layers of the Calizas de La Huérguina Formation date to 129.4 million years ago, making Gorgonavis the oldest entantiornithean known with a substantially elongated rostrum.

facts.statement: Gorgonavis likely belongs to the family Longipterygidae, a group previously known only from China.
facts.quote: Gorgonavis likely belongs to the family Longipterygidae, otherwise definitively known only from China.

facts.statement: Skull anatomy suggests Gorgonavis belongs to the family Longipterygidae, which includes two subfamilies: Longipteryginae and Longirostravinae.
facts.quote: Various anatomical characters of the skull are consistent with the enantiornithean family Longipterygidae, which is traditionally split into two subfamilies: Longipteryginae and Longirostravinae.

facts.statement: Gorgonavis possesses a unique mix of traits from both Longipteryginae and Longirostravinae, making its precise classification uncertain.
facts.quote: Gorgonavis has a unique combination of traits seen in both of these families, making its precise classification somewhat tentative.

facts.statement: Researchers treat the placement of Gorgonavis within Longipterygidae with caution because many defining traits of the group are found in the postcranial skeleton, which is missing in Gorgonavis.
facts.quote: Nebreda et al. (2026) treated a longipterygid placement for Gorgonavis with caution, given that many of the synapomorphies (shared traits) of this group are in the postcranial skeleton, which is not preserved in this taxon.

facts.statement: The exact relationships of Gorgonavis with other longipterygids are debated due to its mosaic of traits from both longipterygines and longirostravines.
facts.quote: The relationships of Gorgonavis with other longipterygids is further complicated by the mosaic of traits characteristic of either longipterygines or longirostravines.
